prompt: What does a cumulative flow diagram count for each day?

choices.text: How many items each person finished that day
choices.why: It counts items, never people, and it counts them cumulatively.

choices.text: The average cycle time of the items finished so far
choices.why: Cycle time can be read off it roughly, but it is not what it counts.

choices.text: How many items had reached each column by its end
choices.why: Right. Each line only grows, and the lines stack in the board's order.

choices.text: How many items moved between columns that day
choices.why: Daily movements would go up and down; a CFD's lines never fall.

prompt: Match each measurement to how it is read off a cumulative flow diagram.

pairs.right: the vertical distance between two lines
the slope of the finishing line
the horizontal distance between two lines

right_distractors: the area under the top line

prompt: On 24 July, 71 of the Billing team's items had started and 43 had merged. How many items were in progress?
The merged line rose from 98 on 4 September to 116 on 25 September. What was the throughput in items per week?
Why is cycle time read off a CFD only approximately?

choices.text: Items do not finish in the order they started
choices.why: Right. The horizontal distance pairs the nth start with the nth finish, which are often different items.

choices.text: The chart is drawn in weeks rather than in days
choices.why: It can be drawn daily; the approximation remains.

choices.text: Cycle time cannot be computed from board dates
choices.why: Lesson 2 computed it exactly from the same dates.

choices.text: Little's law does not hold on a cumulative chart
choices.why: The CFD is where the law is easiest to see.

prompt: On a CFD, the band between two neighbouring lines grows thicker week by week. What does that mean?

choices.text: The team is finishing more work than before
choices.why: Finishing faster would steepen the lower line and thin the band.

choices.text: Fewer requests are arriving
choices.why: That would flatten the top line, not widen a band in the middle.

choices.text: The chart has an error in its dates
choices.why: It is one of the commonest real shapes.

choices.text: Work enters that state faster than it leaves
choices.why: Right. That state is a bottleneck, or the queue in front of one.

prompt: On 24 July, 57 items had reached review and 43 had merged. How many were waiting for or in review?
The Billing team's started line is flat from 31 July to 7 August. How should that be read?

choices.text: The team stopped working for a week
choices.why: The merged line rose steeply that week; work was finishing.

choices.text: Old items finishing under the new limit
choices.why: Right. Each developer finished their three items before taking a fourth; a flat line is a question, here with a good answer.

choices.text: No requests arrived that week
choices.why: Arrivals are the top line, which kept rising.

choices.text: Items were being deleted from the board
choices.why: Deleted items would make a cumulative line fall, which it never does here.

prompt: In June and July the deployed line climbs in steps behind the merged line. What does that show?

choices.text: Deployments were failing
choices.why: Failures are in deploys.csv; steps show timing, not outcome.

choices.text: Reviews took longer than development
choices.why: That is a band between to review and merged, not steps after merge.

choices.text: Merged work went out in a weekly batch
choices.why: Right. The pipeline ran on Thursdays; from August the two lines lie together.

choices.text: Items were merged out of order
choices.why: Order does not make steps; batching does.

prompt: Why is one blocked item among a hundred nearly invisible on a CFD?

choices.text: It changes a band's thickness by one item
choices.why: Right. The CFD describes the board as a whole; the ageing chart shows the single stuck item.

choices.text: Blocked items are left out of every CFD
choices.why: It is counted in its column like any other.

choices.text: A CFD only shows finished items
choices.why: That is the scatterplot; the CFD shows every state.

choices.text: The item's line goes flat and hides behind the others
choices.why: Items have no lines of their own; columns do.

prompt: What is the age of an open item?

choices.text: The number of days since it entered the backlog
choices.why: Age counts from the start of work, matching cycle time.

choices.text: The number of days since someone started work on it
choices.why: Right. On the day it finishes, its age becomes its cycle time.

choices.text: How many days it has left until its deadline
choices.why: Age looks back, not forward, and needs no deadline.

choices.text: Its estimate in points converted into days
choices.why: Age is measured, not estimated.

prompt: Why is work item age called a leading measure, and cycle time a lagging one?

choices.text: Age is computed by the board tool, cycle time by hand
choices.why: Both come from the same dates and either can be computed by a program.

choices.text: Age ignores weekends and cycle time does not
choices.why: Both use the same calendar in this course.

choices.text: Age is averaged over a month, cycle time over a week
choices.why: Neither is defined by an averaging window.

choices.text: Age is known now; cycle time only at the end
choices.why: Right. A stuck item shows in age every morning, and in cycle time only once it is done.

prompt: BIL-189 was started on 21 August. How old was it, in days, on the evening of 30 September?
On 15 July every item past the median age was in review. What did that point at?

choices.text: Developers were starting items too slowly
choices.why: Development held the young items; the old ones were past it.

choices.text: The review column had been set up wrongly
choices.why: The column was fine; the capacity behind it was one person.

choices.text: A queue in front of the one reviewer
choices.why: Right. The same finding lesson 2 reached from averages, here on a single morning.

choices.text: Items in review are always older than items in development
choices.why: They are later in the flow, but six of them past the median is a queue, not a rule.

prompt: On 15 July the 85th percentile of recent cycle times was 31 days, so a 27-day-old item was not flagged as unusual. What is the trap?

choices.text: The percentile should have been taken over a year
choices.why: A longer window would mix in more of the same slow system.

choices.text: A yardstick from a slow period makes slow items look normal
choices.why: Right. Age is judged against recent history, and July's history was itself slow.

choices.text: Ages above 25 days cannot be measured accurately
choices.why: Any age is a simple subtraction of dates.

choices.text: Items in review should not be compared with cycle times
choices.why: Age is comparable with cycle time in any column.

prompt: On an ageing chart, what is each dot?

choices.text: An open item, in its column, at its age
choices.why: Right. The bands behind it are percentiles of recent cycle times.

choices.text: A finished item at the date it finished
choices.why: That is the scatterplot from lesson 2.

choices.text: A person, at the number of items they hold
choices.why: The chart shows items, not people.

choices.text: A day, at the work in progress of that day
choices.why: That is lesson 1's work-in-progress chart.

prompt: How does a queue look different from a single stuck item on an ageing chart?

choices.text: A queue shows as one tall dot, a stuck item as many short ones
choices.why: It is the other way round.

choices.text: They look the same, so the chart cannot tell them apart
choices.why: The two shapes are distinct, as July and September show.

choices.text: Only a queue appears; stuck items are hidden
choices.why: The stuck item is the most visible dot of all, if it stays on the board.

choices.text: Old dots crowd one column; a stuck item stands alone
choices.why: Right. July's review column against September's single dot in development.

prompt: Why read an ageing chart from the right-hand columns first?

choices.text: The right-hand columns hold the newest items
choices.why: They hold the items furthest along, usually the older ones.

choices.text: Charts are always read from right to left
choices.why: This order has a reason specific to flow.

choices.text: Items there are nearest done; finishing frees most
choices.why: Right. More is invested in them, and finishing beats starting.

choices.text: The left-hand columns are not part of work in progress
choices.why: Development is work in progress like review.

prompt: The bands behind an ageing chart are the ___ of recent cycle times.
Why did a standup that went round the people never mention BIL-189?

choices.text: Its developer hid it on purpose
choices.why: Nobody hid anything; everybody reported truthfully.

choices.text: Nobody was working on it
choices.why: Right. Going round people reports what people are doing, and nobody was doing it.

choices.text: It was a bug, and standups only cover features
choices.why: Nothing in the format excludes bugs.

choices.text: It had too few points to matter
choices.why: Its size had nothing to do with why it was missed.

prompt: Which policies keep a blocked item visible? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: A blocked item stays in its column, marked, and keeps ageing
choices.why: Right. Moving it to a separate list removes it from every chart.

choices.text: A blocked item counts against the work-in-progress limit
choices.why: Right. Otherwise the limit has a door in it.

choices.text: Blocked items are reviewed once a quarter
choices.why: A quarter is far too late; BIL-189 waited forty days.

choices.text: An item past the 85th percentile gets a named owner for unblocking it
choices.why: Right. Often the tech lead, when the block sits in another team.

prompt: Put the steps of walking the board in order.
items: Ask what that item needs to move today
Move to the next item, then the next column to the left

prompt: A team's ageing chart shows every dot under the median band, and its CFD shows the backlog band growing steadily. What is the situation?

choices.text: Most of the wait happens before anyone starts
choices.why: Right. Young open items and a growing backlog mean lead time is going up while cycle time looks fine.

choices.text: The team has a bottleneck in development
choices.why: A bottleneck would show old dots in a column.

choices.text: Everything is healthy and nothing needs attention
choices.why: The requesters' wait is growing every week.

choices.text: Items are being blocked and hidden
choices.why: Hidden blocked items would not grow the backlog band.

prompt: An item on the ageing chart has just crossed the median band. What should happen?

choices.text: Nothing until it crosses the 95th
choices.why: By then it is already among the slowest items.

choices.text: Its developer explains the delay to the manager
choices.why: The question is what the item needs, not who is to blame.

choices.text: Ask today what it needs to move
choices.why: Right. Asking is cheap while the item is merely past the median.

choices.text: Re-estimate it in points
choices.why: A new estimate does not move the item.
